key_claims.claim: Mage: The Ascension was first published on August 19, 1993, by White Wolf Publishing at Gen Con, making it the third of the five initial World of Darkness games after Vampire: The Masquerade.

The game's central premise is that reality is consensual—the laws of physics exist because humanity collectively believes in them. Mages are those who have 'Awakened' to this truth and can impose their will on reality.

Paradox is the collective force of consensual reality fighting back against mages. It's described as 'the inertia of 8 billion gallons of belief'—mages who perform vulgar magic risk being 'drowned by the current.'

The Order of Reason, predecessor to the Technocracy, was founded in 1325 CE with the Declaration of the Ivory Tower, dedicated to protecting humanity from supernatural predators—specifically mages and the Order of Hermes.
The Council of Nine Mystic Traditions formed in 1466 CE as a reaction to the Order of Reason, uniting diverse magical practices under a common theory of nine Spheres of magic.
Mage: The Ascension was designed to be 'Ars Magica in the Modern World.' The Order of Hermes and the flexible magic system both derive directly from Ars Magica (1987), co-created by Mark Rein-Hagen.

Phil Brucato, lead developer of Mage 2nd Edition and M20, is a practicing pagan who infused real occult philosophy into the game. He has called it 'possibly the most metaphysically sophisticated game ever created.'

The Technocracy evolved from clear villains in 1st edition to morally complex antagonists by Revised edition—they made the world objectively safer and healthier, but at the cost of wonder and human potential for Awakening.

Mage: The Awakening (2005) replaced consensus reality with Gnostic cosmology: magic originates from five Supernal Realms, separated from the Fallen World by the Abyss after Atlantis's hubris broke the connection.

In Awakening, the Exarchs are god-like mages who ascended to the Supernal Realms and now seek to prevent others from Awakening. The Oracles created the Watchtowers to allow humans to still access magic.
Marauders are mages whose Avatars have shattered, trapping them in personal delusions so powerful that reality bends to match their madness. They are immune to Paradox because they've already broken.

Nephandi are mages who have deliberately inverted their Avatars and serve Oblivion—they seek not Ascension but the destruction of reality itself. They may actually be winning the Ascension War through infiltration.

The Matrix (1999) is frequently cited as capturing the Virtual Adept experience of Awakening—a mage realizing consensus reality is a constructed lie. Brucato notes Mage was 'a major inspiration behind the Matrix movies.'
key_claims.confidence: Medium-High (Brucato's claim; influence is widely discussed but not officially confirmed by Wachowskis)

key_claims.claim: Brucato later reflected that the first edition's fear of technology was misguided: 'Technology is magic, and magic is technology... this magical technology has not flattened humanity into homogenized, dehumanized stasis.'
